title: Cart and order schema
idea: The schema maps the Java model to PostgreSQL tables so the database itself refuses overselling, duplicate checkouts and double payments.

analogy.text: A warehouse ledger with two columns per item: units on the shelf and units promised to customers. The clerk may promise only what the shelf still covers.
analogy.breaks: A clerk can misread the ledger; a CHECK constraint cannot.

points: `inventory` keeps `on_hand` and `reserved`; a CHECK forbids reserving more than exist.
A conditional UPDATE checks and reserves stock in one atomic statement.
Partial unique indexes allow one active cart and one successful payment.
The `orders_unpaid` partial index serves the sweeper's search for late orders.

steps.caption: One T-shirt is left: on_hand 1, reserved 0. Two checkouts start together.
OR-1 runs the conditional UPDATE. The row matches, so it is updated and locked.
OR-2 runs the same UPDATE on the same row. It must wait for the lock.
OR-1 inserts its order rows and commits. The lock is released.
PostgreSQL rechecks OR-2's WHERE clause on the new row. No unit is free, so zero rows match.
Zero rows means out of stock. OR-2 rolls back and reserves nothing.

code.title: Tables and constraints
code.caption: The full schema on a real PostgreSQL 18, then six bad writes the database refuses by itself.

walk.text: Product price as BIGINT paise; inventory with a named CHECK tying reserved to on_hand.
A cart status is TEXT with a CHECK; a partial unique index allows one ACTIVE cart per user.
One `cart_item` row per SKU per cart; quantity is capped at ten.
`orders` (ORDER is a keyword), an Idempotency-Key unique per user, and indexes for order history and the sweeper.
`order_item` copies the unit price, so later price changes leave old orders alone.
Many payment attempts per order, but only one SUCCEEDED row.
Each bad write prints the Postgres error code and the constraint that stopped it.

code.title: Reserve, sweep, pay
code.caption: Two parallel checkouts race for the last T-shirt; then a sweeper frees unpaid stock. Uses trimmed tables so the flow stays short.

walk.text: Reserve each line in SKU order with a conditional UPDATE: check and write in one step.
Zero rows updated means short stock: roll back every earlier line too.
Insert the order with a fifteen-minute payment window, then commit.
Two clients race in parallel; print the sorted results, never who won.
A two-line order fails on the T-shirt; its mug reservation is rolled back.
One statement cancels late orders and returns their units to stock.
Paying is a conditional transition too: in time, but cancelled, so zero rows.

pitfalls: Never check stock with a plain SELECT, then UPDATE; put the check in WHERE.
Pass `now` as a parameter in tests; calling `now()` makes expiry tests flaky.
Name a table `orders`, not `order`; ORDER is a reserved word in SQL.

quiz.q: What does reserve.mjs print for OR-3?
quiz.why: The race already reserved the only T-shirt. The mug line succeeds first, the T-shirt update matches zero rows, and the whole transaction rolls back.

takeaway: Put the stock check in the UPDATE's WHERE clause; keep constraints as the guard.

starters: When would optimistic locking with a version column fit better here?
Should reservations live in their own table instead of a counter?
How do I run the sweeper safely on several servers at once?
